nodes.name: Beyond $\mathsf{W}_2$
nodes.statement: We opted for approximation in the Wasserstein distance because working with distances is convenient. The result could be adapted to encompass the Kullback-Leibler divergence (KL), which is the natural candidate in view of applications. (Note that this would be a stronger approximation result by virtue of , which only requires the second argument in the KL to have a Gaussian moment, guaranteed in our case by working on S^d-1.) To achieve this, after the step involving the disentanglement of supports, we can match the disentangled measures approximately in TV instead of W_2 by following a similar approach to the one developed in , and then apply a reverse Pinsker inequality (see also ). However, to do so, one needs that the measures are mutually absolutely continuous and to have a bounded likelihood ratio. This approach would avoid quantizing the (disentangled) target measure and thus clustering the (disentangled) inputs into atoms.

We opted for approximation in the Wasserstein distance because working with distances is convenient. The result could be adapted to encompass the Kullback-Leibler divergence  $(\mathsf{KL})$, which is the natural candidate in view of applications.

(Note that this would be a stronger approximation result by virtue of \cite{bolley2005weighted}, which only requires the second argument in the $\mathsf{KL}$ to have a Gaussian moment, guaranteed in our case by working on $\mathbb{S}^{d-1}$.)


To achieve this, after the step involving the disentanglement of supports, we can match the disentangled measures approximately in $\mathsf{TV}$ instead of $\mathsf{W}_2$ by following a similar approach to the one developed in \cite{ruiz2024control}, and then apply a reverse Pinsker inequality \cite[Theorem 7]{verdu2014total} (see also \cite{sason2016f}). However, to do so, one needs that the measures are mutually absolutely continuous and to have a bounded likelihood ratio. 




This approach would avoid quantizing the (disentangled) target measure and thus clustering the (disentangled) inputs into atoms.

We look to apply Creflem: tubular.mass.movement separately within each interval, thus, dealing with one measure at a time. Namely, the parameters take the form (bmW,bmU,b)(t)=sum_i=1^N (bmW_i,bmU_i,b_i)(t)1_[T_i-1,T_i)(t), where (bmW_i,bmU_i,b_i) are, roughly speaking, piecewise constant parameters stemming from a repeated application of Creflem: tubular.mass.movement. We critically use to ensure that when we act on the i-th measure in [T_i-1, T_i], all the other measures remain invariant, so mu^i(T_i-1) = mu_0^i. Therefore, we take iin[N] to be arbitrary. We proceed in three steps. subsubsection*Step 1. Partitioning each support into M pieces Let C^i:=supp(mu^i_0), and consider a partition \C^i_k\_kin[M] of C^i consisting of pairwise disjoint sets with connected interiors and satisfying mu_0^i(C_k^i):=alpha_k^i. Namely C^i=bigcup_kin[M] C^i_k with C_k^icap C_k'^i=varnothing if kneq k' (see Creffig: shattering). We now define a target ball contained in C_k^i to which we aim to send the mass contained in the packing . Fix the anchor point x_k^iin intleft(C^i_kright), and let eta>0 be arbitrary and to be determined later on (the same for all indices (i, k)in[N]times[M]), but also small enough so that B_k^i:=B(x_k^i,eta)subsetintleft(C^i_kright). Sending most of the mass to B_k^i [!ht] includegraphics[scale=0.55]figures/figure-3.pdf caption Step 2: packing the piece C_k^i of the partition of C^i=supp(mu_0^i) with balls whose union has mass mu_0^i(C_k^i)-delta. Moreover, mu^i(T_i)=Phi^T_i_\#mu^i_0, and Phi^T_i(x)=x for all xnotin supp(mu_0^i) because of . Using Kantorovich-Rubinstein duality, &hspace0.1cmW_1(mu^i(T_i),mu^i_1) = sup_Lip(phi)leqslant 1left|intphi(mu^i(T_i)-mu_1^i)right|\\ &hspace0.2cm= sup_Lip(phi)leqslant 1left|sum_k=1^Mint_B_k^iphi(mu^i(T_i)- mu_1^i)+int_S^d-1setminus(bigcup_kin[M]B_k^i)phi(mu^i(T_i)-mu_1^i)right|. On the other hand, thanks to , left|int_S^d-1setminus(bigcup_kin[M]B_k^i)phi(mu^i(T_i)-mu_1^i)right|&leqslant 2pi mu^ileft(T_i,S^d-1setminusbigcup_kin[M] B_k^iright)\\ &leqslant 2pi left|1-(1-overlinevarepsilon)^max_kin[M] L_k^isum_k=1^M(alpha_k^i-delta)right|\\ &leqslant 2pi left|1-(1-overlinevarepsilon)^max_kin[M] L_k^i(1-Mdelta)right|, which also tends to 0 as overlinevarepsilon and delta tend to 0. Therefore, we can choose overlinevarepsilon,delta and eta small enough so that W_1left(mu^i(T_i),mu_1^iright)leqslant varepsilon. nodes.statement: We fix iin[N]. Due to , we have supp(nu^i)subset Bleft(x_M^i,Cvarepsilon_1right) for some x_M^iin conv_g\,supp(nu^i) and C>0. Take varepsilon_1 small enough so that kappageqslant 4Cvarepsilon_1. Take x_1^iin partial Bleft(x_M^i,frackappa2right). Consider the minimizing geodesic gamma:[0,1]to S^d-1 between x_1^i and x_M^i, and the function f:[0,1]times [0,pi]&mapsto [0,1]nonumber\\ (s,r)&mapsto f(s,r)=nu^ileft(B(gamma(s),r)right). Since nu^i is absolutely continuous, we have item fin C^0([0,1]times [0,pi];[0,1]). item f(1,r)=1 for all rgeqslant Cvarepsilon_1 item f(0,r)=0 for all rleqslant kappa/2 -Cvarepsilon_1 item f(0,r)=1 for all rgeqslant 1/2+Cvarepsilon_1. By continuity, there exists r^iin (kappa/2-Cvarepsilon_1,kappa/2+Cvarepsilon_1) such that f(0,r^i)=frac1M. Furthermore, due to and we also have nu^j(B(gamma(s),r^i))=0hspace1cm for sin[0,1],\, jneq iin[N]. Finally, note that f(cdot,r^i) is continuous and monotonically increasing provided r^igeqslant Cvarepsilon_1, which is guaranteed by . We can thus pick \s_m^i\_m=2^M-1subset(0,1) such that f(s_m^i,r^i)=fracmM. Hence, the desired balls are Bleft(x_m^i=gamma(s_m^i),r^iright),hspace1cm with (s_1^i, s_M^i)=(0, 1). Finally, since for fixed i, all balls have the same radius, the existence of z_m^i is straightforward.

nodes.name: Proof of \Cref{thm: targets.atoms}
nodes.statement: The proof follows the same ideas as that of Crefthm: main.result, but is significantly simpler since some steps can be omitted completely. Indeed, we can consider Phi^T_fin:=Phi^T_theta_3circPhi^frac2T3_theta_2circPhi^fracT3_theta_1, where item Phi^t_theta_1:P(S^d-1)toP(S^d-1) for tin[0,T/3] is the flow map provided by Crefprop: separation; item Phi^t_theta_2:P(S^d-1)toP(S^d-1) for tin[T/3, 2T/3] is the flow map provided by Crefprop: targets.atoms, which can be applied since Phi^fracT3(mu_0^i) are pairwise disjoint and supported in a single hemisphere for all iin[N]; item Phi^t_theta_3 for tin[2T/3,T] is the flow map provided by Crefprop: interpolation.neural.ode. To conclude, we demonstrate how to derive the bound on the norm of the parameters theta. Recall that by rescaling time, bounding the final time horizon is equivalent to bounding the L^infty--norm of theta. item In the proof of Crefprop: separation, after tracking dependencies one sees that \|theta_1\|_L^infty((0,T);Uptheta)lesssim frac dcdot NT where the implicit constant depends only on the supports of the initial measures. item Once the measures are disentangled, we further cluster them before using Crefprop: interpolation.neural.ode. We thus quantify the convergence in Crefprop: targets.atoms, when bmBequiv0. Specifically, by virtue of Crefcl: cluster.rate, we deduce that for every iin[N], W_2left(mu^i(T_delta),updelta_x_0^iright)leqslant delta with T_delta=O(log1/delta), which implies \|theta_2\|_L^infty((0,T);Uptheta)lesssim logfrac1delta. item Finally, we apply Crefprop: interpolation.neural.ode for the ensemble of atoms x_0^i: since all measures are delta-close to updelta_x_0^i, we have W_2left(mu^i(T),updelta_y^iright)leqslant e^O(1)cdot Ncdot Tdelta, at a cost \|theta_3\|_L^infty((0,T);Uptheta)lesssim fracNT. All in all, W_2left(mu^i(T),updelta_y^iright)leqslant varepsilon, with \|theta\|_L^infty((0,T);Uptheta)=Oleft(fracdcdot NT+log frac1varepsilonright).qedhere

nodes.name: Minimum-exit-time problem
nodes.statement: It is worth noting that the fastest disentanglement problem has a link in spirit with the minimum-exit-time problem (motion with constant velocity). Indeed, for disentanglement to hold, every particle in the support of one measure needs to exit the supports of the other measures. Typically, the minimum-exit-time problem has as input a bounded domain OmegasubsetR^d and x_0in Omega, and one solves minimize T among all alphain L^infty((0,T); R^d) with \|alpha(t)\|=1 for tin[0,T], subject to dotx(t)=alpha(t) & in [0,T],\\ x(0)=x_0,\\ x(T)inpartialOmega. We recall (footnoteThe interested reader is also referred to for an exquisite introduction.) that the solution to this problem is alpha^*(t)=nabla u(x(t)), where u solves the eikonal equation \|nabla u\|=1 & in Omega,\\ u=0 & on partial Omega.

Pi^y) the projection operator onto the first (resp. second) variable. Note that left(Pi^xcircLambda^tright)big(x,ybig)=Phi^t(x)=left( Phi^tcirc Pi^x right)big(x,ybig). Applying Grönwall's inequality, and noting that f(0, cdot)equiv0, we obtain f(t, y)leqslant int_0^te^C_1(t-s)W_p(mu(s),nu(s))\, d s. Therefore, iint d_g(Phi^t(y),Psi^t(y))^pgamma_0(\, d x,\, d y)leqslant C_2^p left(int_0^t e^C_1(t-s)W_p(mu(s),nu(s))\, d sright)^p. where C_2>0 is such d_g(z_1,z_2)leqslant C_2\|z_1-z_2\| for all z_1,z_2in S^d-1, and thus, independent of p. Gathering and in , we find W_p(mu(t),nu(t))leqslant K_1e^K_0tW_p(mu_0,nu_0)+C_2int_0^t e^C_1 (t-s)W_p(mu(s),nu(s))\, d s. Now observe that frac\, d \, d tlangle x(t),omegarangle=Big(-cos d_g(z,x(t)) +cos(R)Big)_+Big(1-langle x(t),omegarangle^2Big), which is positive whenever x(t)inB_0setminus\omega\. We claim that this implies the existence of a time T_varepsilon>0 for which mu(T_varepsilon,B_0capB_1)geqslant(1-varepsilon)mu_0(B_0). To prove this claim, let delta>0 be fixed and to be determined later on. Because of , there exists some T_delta>0 such that Phi^T_delta(x)inB_0capB_1hspace1cm for xin B(z,R-delta), where Phi^T_delta:S^d-1to S^d-1 is the flow map of . Taking delta>0 small enough so that mu_0(B(z,R-delta))geqslant (1-varepsilon) mu_0(B_0) yields claim . We conclude that holds by rescaling time. Finally, by virtue of , the flow map Phi^t is such that Phi^t(x)=x for xinS^d-1setminusB_0 and tin[0,T]. As for the second part of the statement, take B_1=B(omega,eta)subsetB_0 with eta>0 to be determined later on. Owing to , we can argue in the same fashion as in the proof of Crefprop: compression. We have W_1(mu(T_delta),alpha) &= sup_Lip(phi)leqslant 1left|intphi(mu(T_delta)-alpha)right|\\ &hspace0.2cm= sup_Lip(phi)leqslant 1left|int_B_0phi(mu(T_delta)- alpha)+int_S^d-1setminus B_0phi(mu(T_delta)-alpha)right|. On the other hand, left|int_S^d-1setminusB_0phi(mu(T_delta)-alpha)right|=0 by construction. We choose overlinevarepsilon and eta small enough in a way that W_1(mu(T_delta),alpha)leqslant varepsilon.qedhere
